title: Make the error-code vocabulary an enumerable type
description:
The error-code vocabulary becomes a closed enum with a derive-checked member list, so the codes the machine-readable surface reports can be enumerated and mapped to an exit status without a fallback arm.

## Background

The vocabulary is declared as a unit struct carrying associated string constants. Nothing can iterate it, so a twenty-first constant is invisible to any reflection, and the map from code string to exit status ends in a wildcard that classifies an unrecognised code as a generic failure. Neither is there anywhere for a code's meaning to live: no source states what a given code tells its reader, so a reference page for adopters would have to invent that prose. All three properties block later work: a projected reference cannot render a list that does not exist, an exit-status guarantee cannot rest on a map that fails open, and a projection cannot carry a meaning its source does not hold.

The conversion is shape-only. Each code string stays byte-identical on the wire and each existing code keeps the exit status it maps to today, so no consumer observes a change.

The freshness discipline follows the event-tag catalog already in this crate: a public member list beside the type, checked against the variants the type's own derive produces, so a member left out of the list fails the suite rather than being mirrored by hand.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The error-code vocabulary is an enum whose members render the code strings the surface emits today, byte for byte.
- [hard] REQ-02: A public member list enumerates the vocabulary, and a test bound to the type's own derive fails when a member is missing from that list.
- [hard] REQ-03: The member-to-exit-status map is an exhaustive match with no wildcard arm, so a new member is a compile error until its exit status is stated.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each code the vocabulary carried before the conversion maps to the same exit status afterwards.
- [hard] REQ-05: A code arriving as text resolves to its member, and an unrecognised string is reported as unresolved rather than mapped silently.
- [hard] REQ-06: Each member carries a description of the failure it names, supplied by an exhaustive match with no wildcard arm, so a new member is a compile error until its description is stated.

## Notes

The member list is the freshness anchor for later projection work, so it is public rather than private to the module.

planning.outcome: The vocabulary becomes an enum with a derive-checked member list, an exhaustive exit-status match, and a description per member.

title: Register the emitted error codes that carry no exit classification
description:
Error code strings the command surface already prints are absent from the registered vocabulary and fall through to the generic exit status. Registering each one with an explicit exit status is what lets the reported code determine the process exit status.

## Background

Roughly twenty code strings reach machine consumers without a registered exit mapping: namespace-scoped fallbacks across the dependency, gate, preset, item, invariant, project, profile, search, worktree, and hooks namespaces, the claim fallbacks, the generic code itself, and the recovery code. Because none is a registered member, each maps to the generic status whatever its real class.

The status a member takes is the class the plain invocation of the same failure already reports: an unresolvable identifier is a not-found failure, a duplicate gate key is an already-exists failure, a missing preset is a not-found failure. A code whose failure class is genuinely generic keeps the generic status.

Code strings stay byte-identical. Nothing is renamed and nothing is collapsed onto an existing member, because a machine consumer reads the code string and a rename would break it. Only the exit status moves.

The emission sites keep handing the same string literals to the envelope builder; resolving a code from its text into its member is what makes those literals classify, so this work is confined to the vocabulary rather than spread across the dispatch arms.

A parse code is already declared in the vocabulary and carries no exit status yet, so the status it maps to is settled here rather than invented later.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Each error code string the command surface emits is a registered member of the vocabulary carrying an explicitly stated exit status.
- [hard] REQ-02: No emitted code string changes its spelling, and no emitted code is collapsed onto a different member.
- [hard] REQ-03: A registered member's exit status is the class the plain invocation of the same failure reports.
- [hard] REQ-04: A code whose failure class is genuinely generic is registered with the generic status rather than left unregistered.
- [hard] REQ-05: The parse code already declared in the vocabulary carries an explicitly stated exit status.
- [hard] REQ-06: Each newly registered member carries a description of the failure its code names.

planning.outcome: Every error code string the surface emits becomes a registered member carrying an explicitly stated exit status.

title: Expose the stored-record decode failure as a classifiable typed error
description:
A stored-record decode failure is raised as a crate-private type the binary target cannot name, so no downcast reaches it and the failure is reported under the generic code however the classifier is written. Giving that failure a publicly nameable typed form is what lets it carry a registered code.

## Background

The failure occurs when a record on disk cannot be decoded into its in-memory form. The type that raises it is private to the storage layer, so the top level cannot name it in a downcast even though the raising type survives the opaque wrapper it travels in.

Two sites can deliver the change: widening the raising type's visibility, or converting it at the boundary the way one sibling variant is already converted. Widening visibility alone suffices, because the raising type survives the wrapper. Both routes are disclosed, and the criterion states the outcome rather than picking one.

This matters beyond tidiness. Arms that accept no rejectable argument are reached instead through unreadable stored records, so a failure class left unclassifiable keeps those arms unclassifiable with it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A stored-record decode failure is reported under a registered error code rather than the generic fallback.
- [hard] REQ-02: The failure's typed form is nameable from the binary target, so a classifier distinguishes it by type rather than by message text.
- [hard] REQ-03: A repository holding an undecodable stored record produces that code under the machine-readable flag.
- [hard] REQ-04: A record that decodes successfully keeps its current behaviour.

planning.outcome: A stored-record decode failure carries a registered code because its typed form is nameable where failures are classified.

title: Align the search command's exit status with its reported error code
description:
The search command prints a failure envelope and then exits on a literal status its reported code does not map to, so the envelope and the status disagree by construction.

## Background

Both search failures — the search backend reporting an error, and the external search tool being absent — print an envelope carrying their own code and then exit on a fixed value of 10. Neither code maps to 10, so a caller reading the envelope and a caller reading the exit status reach different conclusions about the same failure.

The repair derives the status from the reported code, which is the rule the shared emission macro already follows at every other site.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A failing search invocation under the machine-readable flag exits on the status its reported error code maps to.
- [hard] REQ-02: No exit-status literal remains on the search failure path.
- [hard] REQ-03: The absent-search-tool failure reports a status matching its own reported code.
- [hard] REQ-04: The search-backend failure reports a status matching its own reported code.

planning.outcome: The search failure path exits on the status its reported code maps to rather than a literal.

title: Report per-issue preset failures as a failing envelope
description:
Applying a gate preset under the machine-readable flag nests per-issue failures inside a success payload and exits zero, so an automated caller records a failed application as a success.

## Background

The human invocation exits non-zero when any target issue fails. The machine-readable invocation has no such exit: it serializes the per-issue failures into an array inside the success payload and returns zero. An agent driving preset application therefore has to inspect the payload's contents to notice a failure the plain path signals in the status alone.

The repair reports the failure the way the rest of the surface does — an error envelope carrying a registered code, exiting on the status that code maps to — while keeping the per-issue detail readable for a caller that wants it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A preset application in which at least one target issue fails exits non-zero under the machine-readable flag.
- [hard] REQ-02: That failing application reports an error envelope carrying a registered code rather than a success payload.
- [hard] REQ-03: The per-issue failure detail remains readable from the reported envelope.
- [hard] REQ-04: The failing application's exit status equals the status its reported code maps to.
- [hard] REQ-05: A preset application in which no target issue fails is unchanged in payload shape and exit status.

planning.outcome: A preset application with a failing target reports the error envelope with a non-zero exit status.

title: Verify exit-status parity between the two invocation forms
description:
A caller branching on the process exit status reads a different failure class depending on whether the machine-readable flag was passed. Assertions that drive one failure through both invocation forms and compare the two statuses are what hold them converged.

## Background

Nine failures were measured exiting differently with the flag than without it. An unresolvable identifier exits 3 plain and 1 under the flag in the dependency, claim, and gate namespaces; a duplicate gate key exits 6 plain and 1 under the flag; a missing preset exits 3 plain and 1 under the flag; a preset application with a failing target exits 1 plain and 0 under the flag.

The causes are repaired in the vocabulary and in the individual failure paths. What is missing is the assertion that keeps them converged: no existing coverage drives a single failure through both invocation forms and compares the resulting statuses, which is why the divergence went unnoticed for as long as it did.

The assertions belong beside the existing exit-status coverage, and they compare the two observed statuses rather than restating an expected number per row.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: For a failure reachable in both invocation forms, the plain exit status equals the machine-readable one.
- [hard] REQ-02: An unresolvable identifier reports the not-found status under the flag in the dependency, claim, and gate namespaces.
- [hard] REQ-03: A duplicate gate key reports the already-exists status under the flag.
- [hard] REQ-04: A missing preset reports the not-found status under the flag.
- [hard] REQ-05: A preset application with a failing target reports the same non-zero status in both invocation forms.
- [hard] REQ-06: An undecodable stored record reports the same status in both invocation forms.
- [hard] REQ-07: The assertions compare the two observed statuses rather than a status literal copied into the test.

title: Bind the exit-status projection to the machine-readable invocation form
description:
The generated exit-status reference is bound to runtime through the plain invocation only, so a projected row can be accurate for one invocation form and wrong for the other with no test noticing.

## Background

Each row of the generated reference is exercised by an assertion that drives the command and compares the observed status against the projected value. Those assertions use the plain invocation exclusively. Because the machine-readable path derived its status from a separate and incomplete classification, several rows were accurate for the plain form and wrong for the flag form for as long as that divergence existed, while the projection reported no defect.

Once both paths agree, the binding assertions can cover both forms and hold them agreeing. That closes the projection's blind spot rather than restating documented values a second time.

- [hard] REQ-02: A row whose two invocation forms disagree fails the suite.
- [hard] REQ-03: The completeness assertion still fails when a projected row has no runtime binding.
- [hard] REQ-04: The assertions read the projected value from the projection rather than restating it as a literal.

title: Render the structured envelope from the top-level failure printer
description:
The top-level failure printer renders the structured error envelope for any failure that reaches it under the machine-readable flag, so an arm that propagates its error no longer leaves a machine consumer with an empty payload stream.

## Background

Roughly half the command arms accepting the flag propagate their failures upward with no envelope of their own. The top-level handler writes a human diagnostic line and nothing machine-readable, so a consumer sees an empty payload stream and has to parse prose to learn why the command failed. The generated agent bridge, which drives this surface, reports those failures as a single opaque execution error carrying the diagnostic line inside a shell-command string.

The handler already renders an envelope for three startup failure classes, reading the flag out of the process arguments because those failures precede a parsed command. Broadening that renderer to cover any failure makes envelope presence structural: no path reaches the printer and emits nothing machine-readable, so an arm cannot regress by omission and no per-arm conversion is needed.

The code comes from a classifier over the typed error, built as a structural parallel to the exit-status classifier beside it, so the two remain recognisably the same cascade over the same typed errors. The exit status continues to follow the reported code.

The classifier can only distinguish a failure whose type it can name. One class the probes rely on — an unreadable stored record — is raised as a crate-private type until that type is given a public name, so the classifier is written against a surface where that exposure has already landed; otherwise the arm reached only through corrupted records classifies as generic no matter how the cascade is written.

Failures rejected during argument parsing sit outside this. The argument parser reports them and exits before any command dispatch, on a status that already equals the invalid-argument class.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A failure reaching the top-level printer under the machine-readable flag renders an error envelope on the payload stream.
- [hard] REQ-02: The rendered envelope carries a registered error code chosen by a classifier over the typed error rather than one fixed code.
- [hard] REQ-03: The process exit status equals the status the rendered code maps to.
- [hard] REQ-04: An arm that already renders its own envelope emits exactly one envelope, unchanged in code and detail.
- [hard] REQ-05: The classifier distinguishes each typed error the exit-status classifier distinguishes, so a distinguishable failure is not reported under the generic code.
- [hard] REQ-06: The human diagnostic line still reaches the diagnostic stream while the payload stream carries the envelope alone.
- [hard] REQ-07: A previously propagating arm reports its failure through the envelope with a resolvable code.

planning.outcome: A failure reaching the top-level printer prints an error envelope under a code from a central classifier.

title: Move the recovery command's failure envelope onto the payload stream
description:
The recovery command writes its failure envelope to the diagnostic stream, compactly serialized, under a code outside the registered vocabulary. It moves onto the payload stream so a machine consumer finds the envelope where the rest of the surface puts it.

## Background

Other emission sites print the envelope to the payload stream, in the shared pretty serialization, under an upper-case registered code, exiting on the status that code maps to. This one writes to the diagnostic stream — the stream that carries plain diagnostics everywhere else — serializes compactly, uses a lower-case code no consumer can resolve, and exits on a literal.

A machine consumer reading the payload stream for the envelope therefore finds nothing, and one parsing the diagnostic stream finds a JSON document mixed in with prose. Bringing this site onto the convention is what leaves the payload stream carrying the envelope alone across the surface.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A failing recovery under the machine-readable flag writes its envelope to the payload stream.
- [hard] REQ-02: The envelope uses the shared serialization rather than a compact one.
- [hard] REQ-03: The reported code is a registered member of the error-code vocabulary.
- [hard] REQ-04: The exit status equals the status the reported code maps to, with no literal on the path.
- [hard] REQ-05: The diagnostic stream carries no JSON document for this failure.

planning.outcome: The recovery failure envelope prints on stdout in the shared serialization under a registered code.

title: Report the server control's failures as the error envelope
description:
The server control's start, stop, and status failures print a JSON object of their own shape under the machine-readable flag and exit a literal status, so a consumer that decodes the failure envelope everywhere else cannot decode this one.

## Background

Each of the three failure branches prints a pretty-serialized object carrying a status field and a message string to the payload stream, then exits 1. The payload is machine-readable, but it is not the error envelope: it carries no error code, so nothing identifies the failure class, and the exit status is a literal rather than the class a reported code determines.

The rest of the surface reports failure as an envelope on the payload stream under a registered code, exiting on the status that code maps to. Bringing these three branches onto that convention is what leaves no arm accepting the flag whose failure an agent consumer can read but not classify.

Only the failure branches move. The running-status report, the not-running report, and the start confirmation keep the shape and the exit status they have, because their payloads are already the success side of the contract.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-02: A failing server stop reports the error envelope on the payload stream under a registered error code.
- [hard] REQ-03: A failing server status check reports the error envelope on the payload stream under a registered error code.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each of those three failures exits on the status its reported code maps to, with no exit-status literal left on the failure path.
- [hard] REQ-05: The payload stream carries the error envelope alone for these failures, with no second object shape beside it.
- [hard] REQ-06: The success payloads of the start, stop, and status reports keep their shape and their exit status.
- [hard] REQ-07: Coverage drives each of the three failure branches and asserts the envelope with its code and the exit status that code determines.

title: Failure-lever survey for the issue namespace
description:
The sixteen arms of the issue namespace are surveyed one arm at a time: each is driven into a failure raised inside the arm's own body, and the invocation is recorded in a machine-readable registry fragment for this namespace.

## Background

Whether an arm can be driven into a failure raised inside its own body is unresolved for most of the command surface, and the checks over the machine-readable failure contract rest on the answer. An arm that rejects a malformed identifier fails inside its own body, which is the class the failure contract covers. Running outside a repository instead fails during repository discovery, before any arm body runs, and that path already renders an envelope today — so an arm resolved that way passes against an unmodified binary and proves nothing about the arm. Unreadable stored records are the candidate lever for arms that accept no rejectable argument, because they fail inside the body.

Four arms already render an envelope for an unresolvable identifier, so their lever is a rejectable argument. The creation, batch-creation, search, and listing arms take no identifier that can be made invalid, so their lever has to come from elsewhere.

The fragment is machine-readable rather than prose, because the probes that consume it are code. Each entry carries the command path as the argument parser spells it, the argument vector of the invocation, the setup that invocation needs, and the failure it is expected to produce; an arm with no constructible in-body failure carries an exemption reason in place of an invocation.

The deliverable is the record rather than coverage. Where no in-body failure is constructible, that is the finding, stated with its reason, so that a coverage requirement written later rests on a measured universe.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The fragment states, for each arm of the issue namespace that the command definitions declare with the machine-readable flag, the invocation that drives it into a failure raised after dispatch inside the arm's own body.
- [hard] REQ-02: Each entry states the setup its invocation needs, so the failure is reproducible from the fragment alone.
- [hard] REQ-03: Each entry states the failure its invocation is expected to produce.
- [hard] REQ-04: An arm with no constructible in-body failure carries an exemption reason in place of an invocation rather than being omitted.
- [hard] REQ-05: Re-running a recorded invocation under its recorded setup reproduces the recorded failure.
- [hard] REQ-06: The fragment parses as the shared registry shape and carries no entry outside the arms of the issue namespace.
- [hard] REQ-07: The fragment distinguishes a lever confirmed by invocation from one read out of the source alone.

planning.outcome: A registry fragment records the failure lever for each arm of the issue namespace.

terminal.test_boundary: re-running each recorded invocation in this fragment against its recorded outcome
terminal.worker_sized_reason: Sixteen arms of one namespace are driven once each, with the outcome written into one fragment.

title: The canonical failure-lever registry the probes read

## Background

The failure lever for an arm is measured rather than derived, and the measurement is split by namespace so each survey stays bounded. What the probes need is the opposite of that split: one registry, in one place, covering the whole flag-accepting surface.

The arm universe is derivable — the leaf commands whose definition declares the machine-readable flag, read out of the argument parser's own command reflection — so the registry can be compared against it, and an arm present in the reflection but absent from the registry is a hole rather than an omission nobody notices. The comparison is the same set-equality shape the exit-status projection already uses for its own rows.

The registry lands in the test tree rather than beside the survey fragments, because a probe that read its input from the planning directory would break when that directory is archived. The fragments stay where they were written, as the measurement record; the merged registry is the only one anything reads.

Entries are merged without reinterpretation: a lever recorded by a survey reaches the registry as it was recorded, so a disagreement between the registry and the measurement is a merge defect rather than a judgement call.

title: A shared fixture that drives one recorded failure per command arm
description:
One shared fixture drives a named command arm into the failure the registry records for it and returns its streams with its exit status, so the checks over the machine-readable failure contract share one way of provoking a failure instead of each inventing its own.

## Background

No shared subprocess runner exists in this crate's test tree. Sixty test files resolve the binary and set up a temporary repository themselves, in two competing idioms. Several checks over the failure contract need the same thing — a named arm driven into a failure, with its streams and status captured — so that setup belongs in one fixture rather than repeated in each of them.

Which failure is provoked decides whether a probe proves anything, and that question is settled before this work rather than inside it. A committed registry beside the probes states, per arm, the invocation that reaches a failure raised after dispatch inside the arm's own body, the setup that invocation needs, the failure it is expected to produce, and — for an arm where no such failure is constructible — an exemption reason in its place. The fixture deserializes that registry and drives what it says. It decides no reachability of its own and widens the recorded universe by nothing.

An arm the registry marks as exempt is carried as a declared exemption with the recorded reason, so it stays visible rather than becoming silently absent.

Failures the argument parser rejects are out of scope: the parser reports and exits before dispatch, so the fixture forces failures occurring after dispatch, which is the class the failure contract covers.

The fixture is a module inside the existing issue CLI integration target. That target already aggregates the machine-contract suites, and the build-footprint budget leaves a single integration-target slot, so a dedicated target would spend it on one file.

- [hard] REQ-01: A caller names a command arm and receives its payload stream, its diagnostic stream, and its exit status from one forced failure.
- [hard] REQ-02: The invocation an arm is driven through, and the setup it runs under, are the ones the registry records for that arm.
- [hard] REQ-03: The forced failure occurs after command dispatch rather than during argument parsing.

title: The canonical conformance suite for the machine-readable failure envelope
description:
One suite is the canonical contract for the failure envelope: it drives each probed command arm into a failure and asserts the envelope's structure with its classification as semantic properties.

## Background

The success side of the machine-readable contract has canonical suites — one for the collection wrapper, one for cross-surface field naming. The failure side has none. The nearest file covers five arms, and two of its tests are non-binding: one parses the payload stream and discards the result, leaving only an assertion that the stream is valid JSON, and the other accepts a match on either stream, so it passes whether or not the envelope is emitted. Both pass against the defect this work repairs, so they read as coverage without providing it.

Assertions rest on semantics. The suite asserts that a failure yields an envelope carrying a resolvable code with a non-empty message, that the optional detail and suggestion fields are shaped as declared when present, and that the code identifies the failure class — not that the message equals a particular sentence. The one place a literal field inventory belongs is this suite, as the canonical statement of an intentionally stable external contract.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A single suite is the canonical statement of the failure envelope's contract, identified as such in its module documentation.
- [hard] REQ-02: Each probed command arm is driven into a failure and asserted against the envelope contract.
- [hard] REQ-03: Assertions rest on envelope structure with error classification rather than on copied message text.
- [hard] REQ-04: The test that discarded its parsed payload asserts the envelope contract instead.
- [hard] REQ-05: The test that accepted a match on either stream asserts the envelope on the payload stream alone.
- [hard] REQ-06: A probed failure that emits no envelope fails the suite.

planning.outcome: One suite asserts envelope structure semantically for each probed arm, replacing two vacuous tests.

title: A coverage guard that fails when a command arm has neither a probe nor an exemption
description:
The set of command arms accepting the machine-readable flag is derived from the command definitions and compared against the set the failure probes cover, so an arm added later cannot ship without a probe or a declared exemption behind it.

## Background

A census of which arms render the envelope goes stale the moment a new arm is added, so the durable half of this work is the check rather than the census. The command schema already reflects the command definitions through the argument parser's own introspection: it walks the command tree and records each arm together with the flags declared on it. Deriving the arm set from that reflection leaves no hand-maintained list to drift.

Scope is each arm whose definition declares the flag, with no visibility predicate applied. A hidden arm still runs and still accepts the flag, so filtering to visible arms would turn a later promotion into a silent coverage gap. An arm carried as a declared exemption, recorded with the reason no in-body failure is constructible for it, is covered by that exemption, which the check reports rather than hides.

Completeness is a set equality, following the pattern the exit-status projection already uses: a derived set on one side, the registered set on the other, an inequality failing the build. Beside it, each probe's observed code is asserted to be a registered member other than the generic fallback, so an arm producing an envelope with no real classification is a failure rather than a pass. Where a probe exposes a typed error the central classifier does not distinguish, the classifier gains that arm.

The per-arm result is what satisfies the census obligation: it is derived at check time from the definitions rather than committed as a table that would go stale.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The arm set is derived from the command definitions rather than from a hand-written list.
- [hard] REQ-02: Derivation selects each arm whose definition declares the machine-readable flag, applying no visibility predicate.
- [hard] REQ-03: A newly declared arm with neither a registered failure probe nor a declared exemption fails the check.
- [hard] REQ-04: A registered probe naming an arm the definitions no longer declare fails the check.
- [hard] REQ-05: Each probed arm's forced failure reports a registered error code other than the generic fallback.
- [hard] REQ-06: The check reports, per arm, whether its failure rendered the envelope and under which code.
- [hard] REQ-07: The check runs inside the standard test invocation rather than behind an opt-in step.
- [hard] REQ-08: An arm carried as a declared exemption satisfies the check through that exemption, and the check reports the exemption with its stated reason.

planning.outcome: The arm set derived from the command definitions equals the covered set, with each probe reporting a classified code.

title: Pin payload-stream purity on the machine-readable failure path
description:
A failing invocation under the machine-readable flag writes exactly one JSON document on the payload stream and nothing else, asserted across the probed command arms rather than held by convention.

## Background

The stream split is deliberate: the envelope goes to the payload stream and the human diagnostic to the diagnostic stream, a division existing coverage already pins. Measurement across the arms that could be driven into a failure found payload-stream purity already holding, with one emission site as the exception.

It holds by construction, though, not by assertion. The human output helpers are suppressed under the flag and progress output sits behind flag guards, but nothing fails if a future arm prints an unguarded line ahead of a fallible call.

Suppressing the diagnostic line is not the intent. The contract is that the payload stream carries the envelope alone, which is what a parser reading that stream depends on.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: For a probed arm's forced failure, the payload stream parses as exactly one JSON document.
- [hard] REQ-02: A non-JSON byte on the payload stream fails the check.
- [hard] REQ-03: Output preceding the envelope on the payload stream fails the check.
- [hard] REQ-04: The human diagnostic on the diagnostic stream stays present and is not asserted away.

planning.outcome: A failing flag invocation writes one JSON document on stdout with no plain-text byte beside it.

title: A generated adopter reference for the error-code vocabulary
description:
The error-code vocabulary reaches adopters as a generated reference page projected from the vocabulary itself, listing each code with its meaning and the exit status it maps to.

## Background

No adopter page enumerates the error codes. Individual codes appear in worked examples across several pages, so a reader who receives an unfamiliar code has nowhere to look it up. A hand-written table would be a copy of a fact whose source of truth is the vocabulary in the binary, and would go stale on the first addition. Both columns the page carries — the meaning and the exit status — are read from the vocabulary, which holds a description per member alongside its exit class, so the page renders its source rather than authoring prose beside it.

The projection follows the pattern this crate already uses for its other generated reference pages: a rendering function beside the definitions, a committed page carrying a generated banner, and a test asserting the committed file equals the rendered output byte for byte, with an explicit regeneration path. Because the vocabulary is a closed enum with a derive-checked member list, the page cannot omit a code without failing that check.

The exit-status column is read from the same map the runtime uses, so the page states the mapping rather than restating it. A separate hand-listed enumeration in the output layer does not break when a status is added; this page introduces no second instance of that hazard.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A committed adopter reference page lists each error code with its meaning and its exit status.
- [hard] REQ-02: The page is rendered from the error-code vocabulary rather than hand-written, and carries a generated banner.
- [hard] REQ-03: A test fails when the committed page differs from the rendered output.
- [hard] REQ-04: Adding a member to the vocabulary without regenerating the page fails that test.
- [hard] REQ-05: The exit-status column is read from the runtime mapping rather than restated beside it.
- [hard] REQ-06: The page is reachable from the documentation index alongside the other reference pages.
- [hard] REQ-07: The page cites no path under the planning artifact directory.
- [hard] REQ-08: Each code's meaning is read from the vocabulary's own description rather than authored on the page.

planning.outcome: The error-code vocabulary projects into a committed reference page whose freshness is asserted byte for byte.

title: An enumerable error-code vocabulary with class-correct exit status
description:
The error codes the machine-readable surface reports become an enumerable, closed vocabulary in which each member carries an explicit exit status, so the status a caller observes matches the failure class the envelope names.

## Background

The vocabulary is declared as string constants that cannot be iterated, and the map from code to exit status ends in a wildcard. Roughly twenty code strings the surface actually emits are absent from it, so each exits on the generic status whatever its real class.

Measured against the plain invocation of the identical failure, nine arms disagree: unresolvable identifiers, a duplicate gate key, and a missing preset all report one status without the flag and the generic status with it. One command exits on a literal its own reported code does not map to, and one reports failure inside a success payload with a zero status.

The generated exit-status reference documents the plain values and binds each row to runtime through the plain invocation alone, so the projection is accurate for one invocation form and silently wrong for the other.

One emitted failure class cannot be registered inside the output layer at all: an unreadable stored record is raised as a crate-private type the binary cannot name, so it reports the generic code however the classifier is written.

Code strings stay byte-identical throughout. Nothing is renamed and nothing is collapsed, because a machine consumer reads the code string; only the exit status moves, toward the class the plain path already reports.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The error-code vocabulary is enumerable and maps each member to an exit status with no fallback arm.
- [hard] REQ-02: Each code string the command surface emits is a registered member, unchanged in spelling.
- [hard] REQ-03: For a failure reachable in both invocation forms, the two exit statuses are equal.
- [hard] REQ-04: No command's failure path exits on a literal status its reported code does not determine.
- [hard] REQ-05: The generated exit-status reference is bound to runtime through both invocation forms.
- [hard] REQ-06: A failure raised as a crate-private type is reported under a registered code rather than the generic fallback.
- [hard] REQ-07: Each vocabulary member carries a description of the failure it names, stated once in the vocabulary.

planning.outcome: Every emitted error code is a registered member whose exit status matches the class the plain path reports.

title: Structural envelope emission for every failing machine-readable invocation
description:
Envelope emission stops being per-arm work: the top-level failure printer renders the structured envelope for any failure that reaches it, so no command arm accepting the machine-readable flag can fail without producing machine-readable output.

## Background

Nine distinct mechanisms emit the envelope today — a shared macro, five named helpers, and thirty-five inline sites — each classifying the error at its own call site. Roughly half the arms accepting the flag use none of them and propagate their failures to the top-level handler, which writes a human diagnostic line and leaves the payload stream empty. Several arms that do emit an envelope classify one error class and propagate the rest.

Converting arm by arm would leave the property resting on convention, with nothing structural stopping the next arm from omitting it. Rendering from the top-level printer instead makes envelope presence unmissable, because the printer that used to produce plain text alone becomes the renderer.

Two emission sites remain individually wrong and move onto the convention: one writes its envelope to the diagnostic stream, compactly serialized, under an unregistered code, and the server control writes a machine-readable object of its own shape carrying no code at all, exiting a literal status.

Failures the argument parser rejects sit outside this: the parser reports and exits before dispatch, already on the invalid-argument status.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A failure reaching the top-level printer under the machine-readable flag renders an error envelope on the payload stream.
- [hard] REQ-02: The rendered code comes from a classifier over the typed error rather than one fixed value.
- [hard] REQ-03: An arm that already renders its own envelope keeps its code and detail, emitting exactly one envelope.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each emission site writes the envelope to the payload stream in the shared serialization under a registered code.
- [hard] REQ-05: The process exit status follows the reported code at every emission site.
- [hard] REQ-06: No failing invocation under the flag reports a machine-readable payload of a shape other than the error envelope.

planning.outcome: Envelope presence becomes structural at the top-level printer, and the last off-convention emission site conforms.

title: Per-arm failure conformance and the guard that keeps it
description:
Regression coverage drives each command arm accepting the machine-readable flag into a real failure and asserts the envelope contract, and a guard derived from the command definitions fails when an arm has no such coverage, so a newly added arm cannot ship without the failure contract.

## Background

The success side of the machine-readable contract has canonical suites; the failure side has none. The nearest file covers five arms, and two of its five tests are non-binding — one discards its parsed payload, the other accepts a match on either stream — so both pass against the defect this work repairs.

Whether an arm renders the envelope cannot be decided from the source text. Dispatch bodies mix propagation, inline classification, and helpers that exit internally, and three namespaces already use a wrapper that classifies centrally while its inner function propagates freely, so a scan of a dispatch arm sees a classified call it cannot distinguish from an unclassified one. The property is observable only by running the command.

Provoking a failure is not uniform either: a substantial minority of arms take no argument that can be made invalid and are reached instead through unreadable stored records, which still fails inside the arm body. Whether each arm has such a lever is measured first, namespace by namespace, and merged into one machine-readable registry reconciled against the reflected arm universe, so the coverage requirement is written against a measured surface; one shared fixture then drives what the registry states, and the conformance checks consume it.

Coverage completeness comes from the command definitions themselves, through the introspection the command schema already performs, so no hand-maintained arm list exists to drift.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: One canonical suite asserts the failure envelope's structure with its classification for each probed arm, semantically rather than against copied message text.
- [hard] REQ-02: The arm set the checks cover is derived from the command definitions, with no visibility predicate applied.
- [hard] REQ-03: An arm declaring the machine-readable flag with neither a failure probe nor a declared exemption fails the check.
- [hard] REQ-04: A failing invocation's payload stream carries exactly one JSON document and no plain-text byte.
- [hard] REQ-05: The two non-binding tests assert the envelope contract instead of passing vacuously.
- [hard] REQ-06: The checks report, per arm, whether its failure rendered the envelope and under which code.
- [hard] REQ-07: An arm with no constructible in-body failure is covered by a declared exemption stating its reason rather than by an absent probe.
- [hard] REQ-08: The probes read one registry whose arm set is reconciled against the command definitions.

planning.outcome: Each flag-accepting arm is probed into a real failure or exempt for a recorded reason, and an uncovered new arm fails the build.
